Refugee Roulette

By: Busisiwe Gumede | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Uncovering widespread corruption in South Africa's refugee system, where asylum seekers are forced to pay bribes to secure their status.

Unique Selling Point:
Undercover footage reveals a web of corruption involving Home Affairs officials and external agents, who are exploiting vulnerable individuals fleeing conflict and persecution.


Summary:
The Refugee Appeals Authority of South Africa (RAASA) is facing a staggering backlog of 133,582 appeals, leaving many genuine asylum seekers in limbo. How it works is, an individual arrives into the country and goes straight to the home affairs office and claims to need asylum. Home Affairs is compelled to give you three months, with hardly any investigation done about whether or not you deserve one. Then from there you have to apply every three moths and if HA says no, you are allowed to appeal. So that’s the baglog that I am referring to I’m referring to. Meanwhile, those with the means to pay are able to buy their way to asylum status, regardless of their eligibility.

My research is focused on the Home Affairs Marabastad office in Pretoria, where agents are working in cahoots with officials to sell asylum statuses for R1500. I have sent spy cam footage of these agents and officials negotiating bribes and making demands for payment.

But it's not just the corruption that's alarming - it's the human cost. We spoke to the Moyo family, who were told they would be deported despite having lived in South Africa for years and contributing to the economy. The wife, a critical care nurse with a master's degree, was refused refugee status indefinitely, leaving her family's future uncertain.

Immigration lawyer Claryn Ferreira is fighting for justice, representing families like the Moyos and demanding answers from Home Affairs officials. Our footage captures her confrontation with a supervisor, who fails to provide valid explanations for the corruption.


Further information:
This story exposes the dark underbelly of South Africa's refugee system, where corruption and greed are prioritized over the protection of vulnerable lives. We aim to spark a national conversation about the need for reform and accountability in the refugee system.

Key questions to be explored:

- How widespread is corruption in South Africa's refugee system?
- What are the consequences for genuine asylum seekers who cannot afford to pay bribes?
- How can the system be reformed to ensure accountability and transparency?

Press Release:


Refugee Roulette
Backlogs, red tape, and exploitation: that’s what greets asylum seekers at South Africa’s borders. The law requires refugees to renew their applications every three months. But it’s not enough to jump through hoops: it’s pay up – or get out. As Home Affairs juggles a backlog that’s left hundreds of thousands in limbo, we uncover a web of corrupt officials and agents allegedly exploiting those fleeing conflict and persecution in their home countries. And as deportation looms, families who have called South Africa their home for decades pay the human cost.
Producer: Busisiwe Gumede | Presenter: Masa Kekana

Script:


(Masa) Last month, investigators swooped on the Marabastad Home Affairs office in
Pretoria in a covert operation.
(Upsound Newscast) Now Breaking news: Six Home Affairs officials, linked to fraud and
corruption, have been fired with immediate effect.
(Masa) Perhaps coincidentally, one of them was an official we’d had in our sights for
months.
(Hidden Camera Subtitle) How much do you have?
(Hidden Camera Subtitle) R1700.
(Masa) Marabastad Home Affairs: it’s as infamous for its corruption as it is for its long
queues.
(Masa) We heard reports of asylum seekers being exploited and began a months-long
investigation.
(Frank Gasibamba Subtitles) You can apply and apply and apply but not any response.
(Masa) It's no secret that South Africa has porous borders leading to an immigration
problem. However, there are those people coming to South Africa seeking refuge from
war-torn countries. And for those people trying to seek asylum, legally, it seems the
system is failing even them.
(Masa) Home Affairs is making a point of cracking down on corruption at Marabastad:
bribes demanded to process asylum applications. But the raid failed to touch a vital
element: informal agents, who operate outside the facility.
(Masa) To understand the system, we teamed up with a seasoned whistleblower who
also happens to be an asylum seeker.
(Anonymous Subtitles) If you want the asylum, it's R4000. If you want refugee status,
it's R8000.
(Masa) Our informant fled persecution after exposing corruption in Zimbabwe. Fifteen
years later, he’s an advocate for asylum seekers' rights in South Africa, focusing on
Marabastad.
(Masa) He captures evidence with the help of a hidden camera.
(Anonymous Subtitles) I was at least able to see how they run their stuff inside, starting
from the outside, and who is involved and who is not involved. So, when we were taken
inside that's when I got to see what was exactly going on.

(Masa) And the first surprise: agents of the corruption machinery mingling with the
crowds outside the building.
(Anonymous Subtitles) All of them, they have got their own guys. Those ladies, they sell
outside. So, whenever you want to communicate with the Home Affairs officials, you
have to go through those ladies first.
(Masa) We decided to try it for ourselves. At first glance, this is an ordinary woman
selling food and drinks outside the branch. But she too has a link inside.
(Producer) The thing is, I don’t want someone who will just take our money and then go.
You know?
(Female Subtitle) No, that's why I go straight to the security. To the security. He knows
where to put you inside.
(Male Subtitle) How much do they charge?
(Female Subtitle) R5000, I don’t want to lie.
(Female Subtitles) That’s what it will cost you if you do it alone, without me. That’s what
you’ll have to pay.
(Masa) One of the reasons this network flourishes is an enormous backlog. In 2023,
over one hundred and thirty thousand asylum applications were waiting to be
processed.
(Hlengiwe Mtshatsha) Some of our clients have waited upwards of 10 to 15 years just to
hear the final decision on whether they qualify to be refugees.
(Masa) Lawyers for Human Rights offer free legal help to asylum seekers. Hlengiwe
Mtshatsha says the delays are illegal.
(Hlengiwe Mtshatsha) Our administrative law very clearly states that decisions that
pertain to yourself need to be issued within a reasonable time.
(Masa) And what happens in the interim?
(Hlengiwe Mtshatsha) They are vulnerable to arrest and detention. And the... I think the
worst-case scenario is them, is an asylum seeker facing potential refoulement, and by
refoulement, that means returning to a country where you might face persecution and or
maybe even face certain death.
(Masa) Behind every stack of files lies a person, each waiting for a chance at a future,
while the backlog grows by the day. With the system overwhelmed, what happens to
those caught in the middle?

(Masa) Now a barber in Pretoria's city centre, Frank Gasibamba fled deady conflicts in
the Democratic Republic of Congo nearly twenty years ago.
(Frank Gasimbaba Subtitles) I passed through Tanzania, Tanzania, Malawi - Malawi,
Zimbabwe, and then I came to South Africa.
(Masa) He’s a regular at Marabastad Home Affairs and says because he objects to
paying a bribe, he doesn't get the best service.
(Frank Gasimbaba Subtitles) Right now, I’m living like this without asylum. Because now
it's already expired. Now we are illegal because Home Affairs, they don't work as they
have to.
(Masa) Frank didn’t anticipate that legalizing his stay in South Africa would be a years-
long battle. Neither did this young lady, who asked that we hide her identity. Her family
fled the DRC at around the same time as Frank.
(Anonymous) I came here when I was very young. I was four, I remember my parents
had to beg and cry and everything like, before I could get the asylum.
(Masa) As a minor, her asylum status was tied to her mother’s - until she turned 18.
(Anonymous) My last asylum, like the one I was using, it expired in 2020 so I could not
renew it.
(Masa) She tried to renew her status on her own but failed. And with that came the end
of a dream. She’d been accepted to study engineering at university - but her admission
was cancelled, and she lost her scholarship.
(Anonymous) It really hurt me. Like I felt like I lost everything that I worked hard for last
year.
(Masa) At the launch of the department's anti-corruption forum in March, Home Affairs
Minister, Dr Leon Schreiber emphasised his top priority: digital transformation.
(Minister Leon Schreiber) No more papers that can go missing or be manipulated.
Because you simply cannot bribe a computer.
(Masa) But Schreiber’s predecessors have made similar promises.
(Masa) And the Minister doesn’t seem to have a very clear picture of what’s really
happening at his Department’s offices.
(Minister Leon Schreiber) Sophisticated syndicates are organized themselves within
Home Affairs to extort and defraud both South Africans and immigrants.

(Masa) What our informant encountered at Marabastad can hardly be described as
sophisticated.
(Male 1 Subtitle) Why are we meeting in the bush?
(Male 2 Subtitle) I'm scared of the cameras at the branch.
(Male 1 Subtitle) Where are the cameras?
(Masa) These middlemen are aware of the CCTV cameras on nearby buildings but not
the hidden camera positioned much closer.
(Male 1 Subtitle) I need an asylum.
(Male 2 Subtitle) Asylum?
(Male 2 Subtitle) From which country?
(Male 1 Subtitle) Zimbabwe.
(Masa) No supporting documents? No problem. Head to the internet cafe across the
road.
(Anonymous Subtitles) You have to have an affidavit that states all your names,
everything. And at least ID copy from your country. Something that shows that it's you,
(Masa) But it doesn't have to be legitimate.
(Anonymous Subtitles) That one, even at the Home Affairs, they are doing everything
the affidavit, you can get it there.
(Masa) So if don’t have?
(Anonymous Subtitles) You can get the affidavit there! For R150
(Masa) So if I come just like this, no name, no paper, nothing, and I go outside there?
(Anonymous Subtitles) They will do everything for you.
(Masa) With fake supporting documents in hand, our informant is ushered inside to
complete his application.
(Male 1 Subtitle) Hello, sir. Are you still at the office?
(Male 2 Subtitle) What did he say? Does he want to speak to me?

(Male 1 Subtitle) Yes, speak to him.
(Male 2 Subtitle) Hello, bra. Should I have money ready for you? R1700? We can talk
about it, there’s no problem.
(Anonymous Subtitles) Then they will tell you to maybe come after a month, or come
after a week. But when you have more money, they can fix everything that same time.
(Masa) How much?
(Anonymous Subtitles) Mostly, if you have money, like R4000 - they do everything same
time. You go out with your paper.
(Masa) Shady officials simply delay or decline the applications of those who don’t pay
bribes, and profit from those who do.
(Minister Leon Schreiber) The message to corrupt officials or members of syndicates is
clear and unambiguous. We are cleaning house and when we catch you, you will be out
of the door within a matter of weeks.
(Masa) So, while Minister Schreiber is rightfully celebrating the arrests of a number of
officials accused of corruption, is he missing the bigger picture? For as long as there are
civilians willing to break the law outside Home Affairs, there'll be officials on the inside
willing to grease the wheels.

(Minister Leon Schreiber) The message to corrupt officials or members of syndicates is clear and unambiguous. We are cleaning house and when we catch you, you will be out of the door within a matter of weeks. (Masa) So, while Minister Schreiber is rightfully celebrating the arrests of a number of officials accused of corruption, is he missing the bigger picture? For as long as there are civilians willing to break the law outside Home Affairs, there'll be officials on the inside willing to grease the wheels.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Uncovering widespread corruption in South Africa's refugee system, where asylum seekers are forced to pay bribes to secure their status.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Undercover footage reveals a web of corruption involving Home Affairs officials and external agents, who are exploiting vulnerable individuals fleeing conflict and persecution.
metadata.Summary: The Refugee Appeals Authority of South Africa (RAASA) is facing a staggering backlog of 133,582 appeals, leaving many genuine asylum seekers in limbo. How it works is, an individual arrives into the country and goes straight to the home affairs office and claims to need asylum. Home Affairs is compelled to give you three months, with hardly any investigation done about whether or not you deserve one. Then from there you have to apply every three moths and if HA says no, you are allowed to appeal. So that’s the baglog that I am referring to I’m referring to. Meanwhile, those with the means to pay are able to buy their way to asylum status, regardless of their eligibility. My research is focused on the Home Affairs Marabastad office in Pretoria, where agents are working in cahoots with officials to sell asylum statuses for R1500. I have sent spy cam footage of these agents and officials negotiating bribes and making demands for payment. But it's not just the corruption that's alarming - it's the human cost. We spoke to the Moyo family, who were told they would be deported despite having lived in South Africa for years and contributing to the economy. The wife, a critical care nurse with a master's degree, was refused refugee status indefinitely, leaving her family's future uncertain. Immigration lawyer Claryn Ferreira is fighting for justice, representing families like the Moyos and demanding answers from Home Affairs officials. Our footage captures her confrontation with a supervisor, who fails to provide valid explanations for the corruption.
metadata.Further information: This story exposes the dark underbelly of South Africa's refugee system, where corruption and greed are prioritized over the protection of vulnerable lives. We aim to spark a national conversation about the need for reform and accountability in the refugee system. Key questions to be explored: - How widespread is corruption in South Africa's refugee system? - What are the consequences for genuine asylum seekers who cannot afford to pay bribes? - How can the system be reformed to ensure accountability and transparency?
